blocks.x: Tom Brown reel one and now Mr. Brown would you mind saying a few words to our radio audience?

There's a big ballyhoo today. Would you like to meet the man that started jazz? He's right here in your city standing fast. You shouldn't believe a word of what you've already heard. They're busy telling lies of what they've heard. Tom Brown started jazz in Chicago, even built the name for jazz. Jazz was never used to music until Brown gave it its advance. The colors are not responsible as the great big ballyhoo. It was done by the north, the kid the south. The colors only play plantation and jazz is the part of swing. You can see how well it has done as they're all having fun telling what they've done to create jazz. It was started in 1915. Don't be fooled. It wasn't until then. Everyone has taken copy and claiming that he's the one. The world is misunderstood. The great point of jazz. There's always room for correction for things done in the past. This is the only way I have to get back at them for something wrongfully done. It's too late to derive any benefits. Let's put it all in song. Give right where right belongs. I just want my public to know the truth. P.S. Tom Brown took the first band to Chicago. You can see how well it has done. This script was composed and written June 3, 1955 by Tom Brown and autographed by all good friends. The signatures. The script. Dominic Alamo. Edward Chance. Pete Palmer. And Arnold J. Loicano. The postscript. Reads. The ray did a lot to perfect this jazz. Gus variated to the strainer's swing. Arnold played the golf air piano. While Bill added tempo to the strain. Tom played a kind of lick here and there. To add to this beautiful tone. Tom, when they're all together, you had the finest jazz in the land.
Well, Art, they all say that I was the one that took the first Dixieland band to Chicago.

So it must be so. This band was later turned into jazz by Chicago local musicians. Well, we had the finest kind of tempo and rhythm that took the world by surprise and started something really big. That it is all over the world today. I've enjoyed the fruits of jazz since 1950. I made a lot of photograph records which have made hits. I've made some good records with Yerkes. Yerkes, Dance Orchestra. Yerkes, Happy Six. Yerkes, Southern Five. Yerkes, Jazz Marimba Orchestra. Ray Miller's Black and White Melody Boys. The Benson Orchestra. Harvey, Wagonon, Bisonoff, and Johnny Wiggs Orchestra. The best records was with Yerkes Orchestra, some with Ray Miller, one with Brownlee and Chalky, Wofferman Call with Johnny Bisonoff. By the way, folks, I composed this number. I've made over 100 recordings with Johnny Wiggs that I think are very good. I am proud of a lot of these recordings and I am still active in the music world. They won't let me retire, you know. I once played an affair out at the Great Lakes training station alongside of John Philip Sousa for the Navy Boys and received applause from Sousa himself. I was invited to appear on television in acknowledgement of who brought the boys' sticks and land bands to Chicago. We were only allowed 10 minutes and I could not give the complete story to the public in that short time. But my story will always be in print. I received a trophy from the New Orleans Jazz Club and on it was engraved that I was the first to introduce jazz in Chicago. My pet recordings are Tiger Rags, Jazz Band Ball, Fidgety Feet, Clarinet Marmalade, Post-Ms. Lament, Shep Man Tour, all by Johnny Wiggs, Wofferman Call by Johnny Bisonoff, Shake Your Little Shoulder by Harry Yerkes, Rose of Spain by Ray Miller. I composed this one also. And a number of others that are very good and two numbers to mention. I recorded on Janette, Victor, Columbia, Vocalion, OK, Commodore, Tempo, and Southland Long Playing Record. I am still willing to do some more recording. I am proud to see that I compose Moorpomal Blues, which is the foundation of Moaning Blues, Bonyard Blues, Livers Stable Blues. I also compose such numbers as Love Dreams, Rose of Spain, Just Jazz, Baster Street Hop, Tiger Rag, Wolf of Man Call, Wonder Where My Easy Ride Is Riding Now, and others. And I am still composing other numbers.
I think this is enough for this interview. See you on the next. Yours, Tom Brown.
Yours, Tom Brown. 된 stuff with

segments.title: Opening of reel one, invitation to address radio audience
segments.summary: The interviewer announces reel one and asks Brown to say a few words to the radio audience.

segments.title: Brown's scripted claim to have started jazz in Chicago in 1915
segments.summary: Brown reads a script claiming he started jazz in Chicago in 1915, complains others took the credit, and reads signatures and a postscript naming his bandmates.

segments.title: First Dixieland band to Chicago, recordings, honors and compositions
segments.summary: Brown says he took the first Dixieland band to Chicago, lists the orchestras and Johnny Wiggs records he made, his pet recordings, the Sousa and trophy honors, and tunes he composed.

segments.title: Sign-off and closing remarks
segments.summary: Brown thanks listeners and signs off.
